result.summary: Pausanias tells how the human sacrifices to Artemis Triclaria began, after Melanippus and Comaetho profaned her temple, and how Eurypylus, driven mad by a statue of Dionysus, ended them as the oracle had foretold. He rejects a rival version in which the Eurypylus of Olenus received the chest from Hercules.

scenes.title: Tomb of Eurypylus and Ionian festival
scenes.summary: Pausanias notes the tomb of Eurypylus and promises to explain it, first describing the Ionians' shared shrine of Artemis Triclaria.

place.name: Patrae, between temple of Laphria and the altar

scenes.title: Melanippus, Comaetho and the sacrifices
scenes.summary: Melanippus and Comaetho, forbidden to marry, couple in Artemis's temple. The goddess sends famine and plague, and Delphi demands the sacrifice of a handsome maiden and youth each year.
scenes.stakes: The lovers risk the goddess's wrath, and the people suffer famine, disease and the yearly loss of youths.

place.name: Temple of Artemis Triclaria near Aroe

scenes.title: Eurypylus ends the sacrifice
scenes.summary: Eurypylus takes a chest containing a statue of Dionysus from Troy, goes mad, and is sent by Delphi to a land with a strange sacrifice. He lands at Aroe, is cured, and the sacrifices stop.
scenes.stakes: Eurypylus risks permanent madness; the youths risk death at the altar.

scenes.title: Rival tradition rejected
scenes.summary: Pausanias dismisses the version naming Eurypylus of Olenus, noting the people of Patras honour only the son of Euaemon.

alias_notes.explanation: The river, once called Amilichus (Relentless), was renamed Milichus (Mild) after the sacrifices ended.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias's reflection that love is felt worth life excuses the lovers.

analysis.text: Love defying human and divine law brings collective punishment, and a prophesied foreign god brings relief.
The story explains a local cult of Artemis and Dionysus at Patras and the end of human sacrifice, and shows Pausanias weighing rival traditions.

language_notes.text: Pausanias defers the explanation, a habit of his: he promises to tell the story of Eurypylus after describing the earlier conditions of the country.
"Antipodes" here means exact opposites; old age is said to be the reverse of youth, especially in attitude toward love.
"Confound human laws" means love overturns social rules and customs, even religious obligations such as the priestess's chastity.
Amilichus means "relentless" or "unappeased", an etymological explanation of the river's name tied to the cruel sacrifices.
The final clause is compressed and ambiguous: love is felt by humans as worth risking life for, so blame is lessened.
Ilium is another name for Troy; the "spoil" is the plunder divided among the Greek leaders after the city fell.
Cassandra, Trojan prophetess whom no one believed, is here imagined discarding the chest as a curse on whichever Greek took it.
Cirrha was the port on the Gulf of Corinth serving Delphi, so Eurypylus landed near the oracle.
Milichus is glossed "Mild": the river's name now reflects the end of the savage rite.
Hercules took part in an earlier expedition against Ilium, in the time of Laomedon, which explains the rival claim.

context_notes.text: Aroe, Anthea and Mesatis were towns that later merged into Patrae in Achaea, a region once held by Ionians.
Virgin priestesses were common in Artemis's cult, since she was a virgin goddess who demanded chastity of her servants.
The Pythian Priestess was the oracle of Apollo at Delphi, consulted by Greek cities in times of plague or famine.
Artemis Triclaria was worshipped near Patrae, where a youth and maiden were sacrificed to her annually, as Pausanias recounts earlier.
Dardanus was the legendary ancestor of the Trojan royal house; Hephaestus was the smith god, so the statue is given a divine pedigree.
Patras (Patrae) was the main city of the region; its local cult honoured Eurypylus within the Dionysus festival.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias generalizes about old age, portraying the parents as unsympathetic and setting generational conflict as the cause of the lovers' defiance.
Divine anger is shown through famine and plague, a common ancient pattern linking human sacrilege to collective suffering.
The innocent youths dying for others' offense, and their grieving relatives, evoke pity and highlight the injustice of the punishment.
Pausanias steps in with a personal judgment, softening blame and showing his reflective, sympathetic stance toward human passion.
The oracle's prophecy of a foreign king and god sets up the events that follow and their fulfilment.
The god's image, which will bring healing and end bloodshed, first drives its finder mad.
The river's new name, Mild, marks the change from cruelty to gentleness.
Pausanias intrudes as a critical historian, rejecting a rival tradition by appeal to what he finds plausible.
